study.title: Ephesians 3 The mystery revealed, the prayer for the inner strength and the final glory of God
study.overview: Ephesians 3 presents two great emphases: first, Paul explains his ministry among the Gentiles as part of God's eternal plan; then he prays that believers may be strengthened inwardly and understand the love of Christ. The chapter ends with a doxology that places all the glory in God, celebrated in the church and in Christ Jesus. The tone is pastoral and theological at the same time: suffering, grace, unity of the church and trust in the power of God walk together.

outline.title: Paul and the mystery now revealed
outline.explanation: Paul presents himself as a prisoner because of his call to the Gentiles. He says that he received the mystery of Christ by revelation: in other generations this was hidden, but now it was manifest by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets. This mystery includes the inclusion of Gentiles as coerdeiros, members of the same body, and participants of the promise in Christ by the gospel.

outline.title: The ministry of grace and the purpose of making known the wisdom of God
outline.explanation: Paul describes his service as a gift of grace, given according to the power of God. He sees himself as the least of the saints, but received the task of proclaiming the unfathomable riches of Christ and clarifying to all the previously hidden plan in God. The expected result is that God's multiform wisdom be known, including by the heavenly powers, and that believers have courage and confident access to God by faith. Therefore, Paul asks not to be discouraged by their afflictions, for they serve their glory.

outline.title: Prayer for strengthening, love and fullness; the final glory
outline.explanation: Paul kneels before the Father and prays that, according to the richness of divine glory, believers may be strengthened by the Spirit in the inner being, that Christ may dwell by faith in their hearts. He asks that they be rooted in love, able to understand with all the saints the greatness of Christ's love and to know something that surpasses understanding. Everything culminates in the confidence that God can do much more than we ask or think; therefore, the glory belongs to him in the church and in Christ Jesus for all generations.

study.context: The chapter resumes and deepens the explanation of Ephesians 1-2 on God's plan in Christ. The notes provided highlight that Paul wrote imprisoned, linked to his testimony among the Gentiles. They also point out that his mission was understood as part of God's eternal purpose and that he combines instruction with prayer, showing that the truth of the gospel should be accompanied by intercession by the listeners.
study.theology: The theological center of the chapter is the revelation of the mystery of Christ: in Christ, Jews and Gentiles form one people, with full participation in God's promises. The church is not only a beneficiary of salvation, but also a visible instrument of God's wisdom before spiritual realities. The chapter also teaches that access to God is entrusted to faith in Christ, not human merit. Paul's prayer shows that Christian growth is not only external, but inner: strengthening by the Spirit, indwelling of Christ by faith, rooting in the love and fullness of God. Finally, doxology states that every power and every answer exceed our petitions, so that the glory of Christian life belongs to God, in the church and in Christ Jesus.

scholarViews.insight: The church, composed of Jews and Gentiles, must fully reflect and express the glory of God.
Paul unites instruction and prayer, showing that his teachings would be useless without the effective cooperation of God by the Spirit.
The chapter culminates with the doxology in which all glory is ascribed to God through Christ Jesus throughout all generations and in eternity.

questions: What changes in the way of seeing the church when we understand that Jews and Gentiles are coercions in Christ and belong to the same body?
In which areas of your life do you need to be strengthened by the Spirit within, and not just receive external help?
How can the confidence that God does much more than we ask or think can shape his prayer and his reaction to difficulties?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to humility and trust. Act concretely in three directions: 1) pray for inner strengthening before asking for only external changes; 2) treat the church as the space where the wisdom of God should be seen in practice, promoting unity among different brothers; 3) instead of discouraging with suffering and limitations, giving God your expectation that it can do more than you imagine. A good application is to separate a time to pray verses 14 to 21 in the first person, turning Paul's prayer in prayer for his own life and for his community.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are brief and do not cover all possible details of the chapter; therefore, some historical and pastoral connections were kept only at the level that the text and comments allow. There is also a small interpretive variation in the notes on the scope of "family" in 3:15; here the central idea of unity under the fatherhood of God was preserved without taking advantage of an exclusive formulation.
